steps.title: Displacement and distance are two different integrals
steps.body:
For a velocity \(v(t)\):
•  displacement from \(t=a\) to \(t=b\): \(\int_a^b v(t)\,dt\) (signed: backwards counts negative)
•  distance travelled: \(\int_a^b|v(t)|\,dt\) (every metre counts)
•  they agree only when the velocity does not change sign

Here \(\int_0^4 v=-1.33\) (ends \(1.33\) m behind the start) but \(\int_0^4|v|=16.2\) m travelled.

steps.title: When is the particle moving backwards (in the negative direction)?
opts: Never: the graph is a parabola
steps.ok: ✓ Right. Below the axis means negative velocity: moving backwards. The particle changes direction at \(t=1\) and \(t=3\).
bads: ✗ Those are the intervals where \(v>0\): moving forwards. Backwards is where the graph is below the axis, \(1<t<3\).
✗ The sign of \(v\) is the direction. The parabola dips below the axis between \(t=1\) and \(t=3\).

steps.title: Where it lives on your calculator
steps.body:

•  displacement: integrate \(v(t)\)
•  distance: integrate abs(\(v(t)\))
•  direction change: zero tool on \(v(t)\)

steps.title: What the three pieces mean
steps.body:
\(v(t)=t^{2}-4t+3\) on \(0\le t\le4\):
•  \(0\) to \(1\): \(+1.33\) m forwards
•  \(1\) to \(3\): \(-1.33\) m (backwards)
•  \(3\) to \(4\): \(+1.33\) m forwards

Displacement \(=1.33-1.33+1.33=1.33\) m. Distance \(=1.33+1.33+1.33=4\) m. The particle ends \(1.33\) m ahead of its start, having travelled \(4\) m.

parts: ✗ Distance: integrate \(|v|\) over the whole interval.

wrongs: \(1.33\) is the displacement. Distance counts the backward piece as positive: \(4\).
\(2.67\) is the two forward pieces only; add the backward piece.

steps.title: What the examiner wants to see
steps.body:
Name the quantity, write the integral, give the value with units:
•  distance \(=\displaystyle\int_0^4|v(t)|\,dt=4\) m
•  displacement \(=\displaystyle\int_0^4 v(t)\,dt=1.33\) m

The modulus sign in the distance integral is a method mark on its own. “Distance = 4” with no integral is an answer without method.

steps.title: Which working earns full marks for the distance travelled?
bads: ✗ That is the displacement: no modulus, so the backward piece was subtracted.
✗ The number alone: no integral, no modulus, no units.

parts: ✗ \(2\cos t=0\) at \(t=\tfrac{\pi}{2}\): forwards before, backwards after.
So the displacement over \(0\le t\le\pi\) is
\(0\): the forward and backward pieces cancel
✗ The two pieces are equal and opposite, so \(\int_0^{\pi}2\cos t\,dt=0\). The distance is not zero.

steps.title: Position: start where you started
steps.body:
If the displacement at \(t=0\) is \(s(0)\), then
•  \(s(b)=s(0)+\displaystyle\int_0^b v(t)\,dt\)
•  the integral is the change in position; add it to where the particle began

\(v(t)=4-t^{2}\), \(s(0)=3\): \(s(3)=3+\int_0^3(4-t^{2})\,dt=3+3=6\) m. The furthest point is at \(t=2\) (where \(v=0\)): \(s(2)=3+5.33=8.33\) m.

parts: ✓ Initial position plus the signed change.
✗ Position \(=\) start \(+\) displacement: \(s(0)+\int_0^3 v\,dt\). The modulus would give distance, which is not a position.

\(10.7\) is \(3+\int_0^3|v|\,dt\): that mixes position with distance.

steps.title: Models: braking to a stop
steps.body:
A car brakes with velocity \(v(t)=20-2t\) m s⁻¹.
•  it stops when \(v=0\): \(t=10\) s (not at the end of some given interval)
•  the stopping distance is \(\int_0^{10}v\,dt=100\) m
•  after \(t=10\) the model would give negative velocity, which is not the car reversing: the model stops applying

parts: ✗ The car travels until it stops: upper limit is where \(v(t)=0\).
steps.givenNote: velocity of a braking car in m s⁻¹
steps.title: Find the distance the car travels before it stops.
instr: Zero of \(v\), then ∫ from \(0\) to that time.
steps.label: distance \(=\)
steps.ok: ✓ \(100\) m (a triangle of base \(10\) and height \(20\)).
wrongs: \(10\) is the stopping time; the distance is \(\int_0^{10}v\,dt=100\).
\(200\) is \(20\times10\): the speed is not constant; integrate (or halve the rectangle).
\(\int_0^{20}v\,dt=0\): the limit \(20\) runs past the stop. Use \(t=10\).
